overview.historicalContext: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic has roots in Euclid's *Elements* (c. 300 BCE): Book VII, Proposition 31 proves every composite number has a prime factor (existence), while Propositions 32 and Book IX, Proposition 14 establish key steps toward uniqueness. However, Euclid never stated the theorem explicitly. Carl Friedrich Gauss gave the first rigorous proof in §16 of his *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae* (1801), recognizing that uniqueness requires Euclid's Lemma ($p \mid ab \Rightarrow p \mid a \lor p \mid b$) as a non-trivial ingredient. Ernst Zermelo (1934) gave an elegant proof using the well-ordering principle. The theorem fails in certain algebraic number rings — for example, in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$, $6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ has two distinct factorizations into irreducibles. Kummer's introduction of 'ideal numbers' (1847) to restore unique factorization led to Dedekind's theory of ideals and ultimately to the algebraic concept of a **Unique Factorization Domain** (UFD). This is #80 on Freek Wiedijk's list of 100 theorems formalized in proof assistants.
overview.problemStatement:
**Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic**:

Every integer $n > 1$ has a unique prime factorization:
$$n = p_1^{a_1} \cdot p_2^{a_2} \cdots p_k^{a_k}$$
where $p_1 < p_2 < \cdots < p_k$ are primes and $a_i \ge 1$.
overview.text: Every integer > 1 is uniquely representable as a product of primes. The cornerstone of number theory.
overview.proofStrategy: The strong induction and Euclid's Lemma proofs are inside Mathlib; this file assembles them into a combined existence-and-uniqueness statement with pedagogical value. Existence by strong induction on $n$: if $n$ is prime, done; otherwise $n = ab$ with $1 < a, b < n$, and induction gives factorizations of $a$ and $b$ which concatenate. Uniqueness follows from Euclid's Lemma (`Nat.Prime.dvd_mul`): two prime lists with the same product must be permutations. The formalization uses Mathlib's `Nat.primeFactorsList` for the canonical sorted factor list.
keyInsights: **Euclid's Lemma** is the heart of uniqueness: $p \mid ab \Rightarrow p \mid a \lor p \mid b$ ensures that each prime in one factorization must appear in any other factorization of the same number

The **algebraic generalization** — $\mathbb{N}$ is a `UniqueFactorizationMonoid` — connects elementary number theory to abstract algebra, where UFDs include polynomial rings $K[x]$ and Gaussian integers $\mathbb{Z}[i]$
**Sorted canonical form**: requiring $p_1 \le p_2 \le \cdots$ makes the factorization absolutely unique (not just up to permutation), which Mathlib's `primeFactorsList` provides automatically
The **coprime disjoint factors** theorem ($\gcd(m,n) = 1 \Rightarrow$ factor lists are disjoint) demonstrates that coprimality has a clean characterization in terms of prime factorizations

The **Finsupp representation** `Nat.factorization` maps each prime to its exponent, giving $n \mapsto (p \mapsto v_p(n))$ — this is often more convenient than the list representation for multiplicative arithmetic

sections.title: Module Documentation
sections.summary: States the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic ($n = p_1^{a_1} \cdots p_k^{a_k}$ uniquely), proof approach via strong induction and Euclid's Lemma, Mathlib dependencies, and historical note (Euclid c. 300 BCE, Gauss 1801, Wiedijk #80).
sections.mathContext: Header for the FTA: every $n > 1$ has a unique factorization $n = p_1^{a_1} \cdots p_k^{a_k}$ with $p_1 < \cdots < p_k$ prime. Proved via strong induction (existence) and Euclid's lemma $p \mid ab \Rightarrow p \mid a \lor p \mid b$ (uniqueness).

sections.title: Existence of Prime Factorization
sections.summary: Proves `n.primeFactorsList.prod = n` (existence), that all factors are prime, and that the factor list is sorted. All via Mathlib's `Nat.prod_primeFactorsList`, `Nat.prime_of_mem_primeFactorsList`, `Nat.primeFactorsList_sorted`.
sections.mathContext: Existence: $\prod \text{primeFactorsList}(n) = n$ for $n > 0$, with every element $p_i$ prime and the list sorted $p_1 \leq p_2 \leq \cdots$.

sections.title: Uniqueness of Prime Factorization
sections.summary: Proves two prime lists with the same product are permutations (`prime_lists_perm_of_prod_eq`), and that equal factor lists imply equal numbers. Uses `Nat.primeFactorsList_unique`.
sections.mathContext: Uniqueness: if $\ell_1, \ell_2$ are lists of primes with $\prod \ell_1 = \prod \ell_2$, then $\ell_1 \sim \ell_2$ (permutation). Follows from Euclid's lemma via `Nat.primeFactorsList_unique`.

sections.title: Complete FTA Statement
sections.summary: States and proves the full theorem: $\forall n \ge 2$, $\exists$ sorted prime list $\ell$ with $\prod \ell = n$ and any other prime list with same product is a permutation of $\ell$.
sections.mathContext: Combined FTA: $\forall n \geq 2,\; \exists!\, \ell = [p_1, \ldots, p_k]$ (sorted, all prime) with $\prod \ell = n$. Any prime list $\ell'$ with $\prod \ell' = n$ is a permutation of $\ell$.

sections.title: Unique Factorization Domain
sections.summary: Proves $\mathbb{N}$ is a `UniqueFactorizationMonoid` via `inferInstance`, connecting to the algebraic theory of UFDs.
sections.mathContext: $\mathbb{N}$ is a unique factorization monoid (UFD): every $n > 0$ factors uniquely into irreducibles. Generalizes to polynomial rings $K[x]$ and Gaussian integers $\mathbb{Z}[i]$.

sections.title: Euclid's Lemma
sections.summary: Proves $p \mid ab \Rightarrow p \mid a \lor p \mid b$ for prime $p$ via `Nat.Prime.dvd_mul` — the key lemma for uniqueness.
sections.mathContext: Euclid's lemma: for prime $p$, $p \mid ab \implies p \mid a \lor p \mid b$. This multiplicative property of primes is the engine of uniqueness: it forces each prime in one factorization to appear in any other.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.summary: Verifies factorizations by `native_decide`: $12 = [2,2,3]$, $30 = [2,3,5]$, $60 = [2,2,3,5]$, $17 = [17]$. Confirms product and sorted properties.
sections.mathContext: Computational examples: $12 = 2^2 \cdot 3$, $30 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$, $60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$, $17 = 17$ (prime). Each verified by `native_decide` with $\prod \ell = n$ and $\ell$ sorted.

sections.title: Corollaries and Applications
sections.summary: Proves prime iff singleton factorization, coprime implies disjoint factors ($\gcd(m,n) = 1 \Rightarrow$ disjoint lists), and connects `primeFactorsList.count` to `Nat.factorization` (the Finsupp representation).
sections.mathContext: Corollaries: $n$ prime $\iff$ $\text{primeFactorsList}(n) = [n]$; $\gcd(m,n)=1 \implies \text{primeFactorsList}(m) \cap \text{primeFactorsList}(n) = \emptyset$; and the Finsupp representation $v_p(n) = \text{primeFactorsList}(n).\text{count}(p)$.

crossReferences.description: Bezout's identity (gcd(a,b) = ax + by) is the key lemma for proving Euclid's lemma (p|ab implies p|a or p|b), which underpins the uniqueness of prime factorization.
The Euclidean algorithm computes GCDs, providing the constructive backbone for the division and factorization steps in FTA.
The existence part of FTA guarantees every integer > 1 has a prime factor; the infinitude of primes shows no finite set of primes suffices for all integers.
Euler's totient function phi(n) = n * prod(1-1/p) is computed from the unique prime factorization guaranteed by FTA.

conclusion.summary: The formalization presents the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic with existence (via `Nat.prod_primeFactorsList`), uniqueness (via `primeFactorsList_unique` and Euclid's Lemma), the algebraic UFD characterization, and practical corollaries including coprime disjoint factors and the Finsupp factorization representation. All proofs are complete with zero sorries.
conclusion.implications: The FTA underpins all of multiplicative number theory: the Möbius function, Euler's totient, the Riemann zeta function, and RSA cryptography all depend on unique factorization. The UFD characterization connects to algebraic number theory, where failure of unique factorization in number rings motivated Dedekind's theory of ideals.
openQuestions: Can the formalization be extended to prove the multiplicative property of the factorization function: factorization(mn) = factorization(m) + factorization(n) for coprime m, n?
Can the failure of unique factorization in Z[√-5] be formalized as a counterexample showing it is not a UFD?
Can the connection to the Riemann zeta function Euler product ζ(s) = Π(1-p^{-s})^{-1} be formalized as a consequence of the FTA?
